newsitem.title: FRANCE: Milosevic, Izetbegovic to announce agreements.
newsitem.headline: Milosevic, Izetbegovic to announce agreements.

text.p: Presidents Slobodan Milosevic of Serbia and Alija Izetbegovic of Bosnia extended summit talks in Paris on Thursday and were expected to announce agreement on "concrete steps" towards normalising post-war relations.

The former enemies held an unscheduled second working session after lunch with French President Jacques Chirac and international mediator Carl Bildt, and set a joint news conference to announce their agreement at 1415 GMT.
Diplomats said they would announce an exchange of diplomatic missions and the opening of telecommunications and air links between their two former Yugoslav republics.

Milosevic told reporters the first meeting with the newly elected leader of Bosnia's three-man presidency "went well". They met at the Hotel de Marigny state guesthouse opposite the Elysee presidential palace.
Bildt's spokesman, Michael Maclay, called the talks "very promising".
Bosnian leaders were more cautious. Izetbegovic said on entering the second working session: "The talks are continuing", and his vice-president, Ejup Ganic, added: "No agreement yet."

French sources said the second session would cover a Bosnian lawsuit against Serbia in the International Court of Justice, France's proposals for a two-year regional stabilisation plan, and the future of the NATO-led IFOR peace force when its mandate expires in December.

Chirac promised that France and the European Union would continue to aid Bosnia's recovery and told Izetbegovic he had "an essential role to play to make peace a success...(and) personify a tolerant Bosnia reconciled at last with itself".

Before the first meeting, the Bosnian and Serbian leaders posed stiffly for photographers at opposite ends of a long Louis XV sofa. They looked more relaxed later, smiled and shook hands at a joint photo opportunity with Chirac and Bildt in the gardens of the Elysee palace.

Savouring a rare trip outside Serbia in the week that U.N. trade sanctions against rump Yugoslavia were finally lifted, Milosevic took a stroll up the celebrated Champs-Elysees avenue on Wednesday night to the Arc de Triomphe monument, flanked by two bodyguards and two French security men.

Bildt said he hoped the leaders would set aside differences over the Bosnian lawsuit and agree on a quick exchange of diplomatic missions, almost a year behind the Dayton timetable. Both sides were also keen to rebuild economic links, he said.

The two presidents signed an agreement in Dayton, Ohio, last November recognizing each other's countries as sovereign states within current borders and agreed "urgently" to establish diplomatic relations and open embassies in respective capitals.
Sarajevo's lawsuit against Belgrade in March, 1993 before the international court in The Hague over alleged Serbian aggression against Bosnia has stalled the process.
The former Yugoslav federal army supported the Bosnian Serbs when they rose against the Bosnian Moslem and Croat bid for independence in 1992.
Belgrade told Sarajevo last Friday that diplomatic relations can not be established with the lawsuit still going on, but Bosnian officials said they would press the case.

Milosevic helped secure the Dayton peace accord by forcing recalcitrant Serb leaders to the negotiating table. But the West expects him to rein in Serb members of the future joint Bosnian government who make no secret of separatist desires.

The West wants the three main players in the Balkan crisis -- Bosnia, Croatia and Serbia -- to normalise relations as soon as possible as a guarantee for stability in the Balkans and a deterrrent against any nationalist drives to break up Bosnia.
Yugoslavia and Croatia recognized each other on August 23.
